item.title: In Confirming Blanche, Senators Endorse a Justice Dept. Under Trump’s Sway
item.description:
The three lame-duck Republican senators who narrowly saved Todd Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general ended up backing him because they believed he was the only person who had earned enough trust, and enjoyed enough access, to rein in President Trump.

One issue with that calculation: Mr. Blanche is a champion of unbridled presidential power.

Time and again during his turbulent nomination process, Mr. Blanche made it unmistakably clear that he believes Mr. Trump possesses a nearly limitless right to directly control the actions of the Justice Department under Article II of the Constitution. It is an argument that formed the foundation of his strategy as the president’s criminal defense lawyer and is the lodestar of his government service.

Mr. Blanche’s confirmation in the pre-dawn hours on Saturday was largely symbolic: as acting attorney general, he could have served indefinitely. But it represented a powerful endorsement by Congress of the philosophy that has guided him under a meddling, demanding boss — that he has a constitutional obligation to execute every lawful White House order, even if it shatters longstanding policy and rule-of-law norms, or contradicts what he thinks is right.

He articulated that view from the moment he took over as acting attorney general in April, telling reporters that Mr. Trump had “the right” and “duty” to order up investigations of people he targets. During his confirmation, both in public and in private conversations, Mr. Blanche sidestepped questions over whether actions Mr. Trump ordered were right, saying only that Mr. Trump had the right to do them.

Barbara McQuade, a University of Michigan Law School professor and former federal prosecutor, said this marked a major break from past administrations. “Just because a president can control the Justice Department does not mean he should,” she said. “Since Watergate, America has prized a Justice Department that is independent from partisan politics.”

While Mr. Trump and allies like Mr. Blanche have repeatedly accused the Biden White House of ordering up prosecutorial hit jobs against Republicans, they have provided little evidence to support the kind of direct interventions that have become commonplace in Mr. Trump’s second term.

In a recent interview, former President Barack Obama said he followed a broad rule of remaining at a distance from the Justice Department to protect its independence, even though he was not legally required to do so.

“The White House shouldn’t be able to direct the attorney general to go around prosecuting whoever the president wants to prosecute,” he said. “The idea is that the attorney general is the people’s lawyer. It’s not the president’s consiglieri.”

Mr. Trump has a different view. Case in point: Late Monday, he browbeat Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, for withdrawing the indictment of a man accused of defacing the Reflecting Pool. While the melodramatic showdown was big news, the fact that the president was issuing marching orders to a federal prosecutor was so typical under this administration it was not noted in most of the coverage.

During his confirmation hearing, Senator Chris Coons, Democrat of Delaware, asked Mr. Blanche whether the department he was running is “independent from the White House?”

Mr. Blanche’s reply: “Article II of the Constitution gives the power of the executive to President Trump.”

When Mr. Coons followed up by asking if he would resign if Mr. Trump directed him do something illegal or unethical, Mr. Blanche said: “That will never happen. But yes, if it were to happen, I’m not going to violate my oath to the Constitution.”

Mr. Blanche shares Mr. Trump’s view that the landmark 2024 Supreme Court ruling that granted Mr. Trump sweeping immunity from prosecution represents a broader endorsement of expanded presidential authority.

“Todd Blanche has lived firsthand the expansion of executive power by the Supreme Court and Trump,” said John P. Fishwick Jr., who served as U.S. attorney for the Western District of Virginia under Mr. Obama. “Look for D.O.J. to aggressively protect this muscular executive power.”

While many Republicans raised questions about Mr. Blanche’s actions and even his independence during his confirmation, few were willing to withhold, or even leverage, their votes to challenge the boss-employee dynamic Mr. Trump has imposed on the department.

“Ultimately, decisions are made by the president,” said Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, who announced in a floor speech Friday that he would deliver the decisive vote for Mr. Blanche’s confirmation.

The adviser Mr. Cassidy consulted before making up his mind was notable. During his speech, he quoted extensively from conversations with William P. Barr, Mr. Trump’s attorney general in his first term who articulated an expansive view of presidential power in a 2018 memo. Mr. Barr quit two years later when pressured by Mr. Trump to help undermine confidence in the 2020 election.

Mr. Barr counseled Mr. Cassidy to support Mr. Blanche in the belief that he could quietly talk the president out of bad ideas, even though Mr. Barr quit rather than comply with Mr. Trump’s demands to investigate an election Mr. Barr found had been fairly conducted.

Mr. Blanche’s experience as Mr. Trump’s private lawyer was not a reason to oppose him, Mr. Barr told Mr. Cassidy — but an asset. It gave Mr. Blanche the capacity to “have tough conversations” and confront Mr. Trump with “difficult truths” that could change his mind, Mr. Barr said to him.

Not every Republican bought into this job description of an attorney general.

Two Republican women, Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Senator Lisa Murkowksi of Alaska, said they would vote no on Mr. Blanche precisely because he had been unwilling to speak truth to Mr. Trump’s power or have enough tough conversations with him.

Ms. Collins, the first Republican to oppose Mr. Blanche, said he had taken several actions “that have further eroded the department’s independence,” including his sign-off of tax protections for the president and his family and the attempted indictments of Democratic lawmakers who criticized Mr. Trump.

Early Friday, Ms. Murkowski, a consistent and plain-spoken Republican critic of Mr. Trump, described her no vote as a moment of major historic consequence — an opportunity to both demonstrate the chamber’s dissatisfaction with Mr. Blanche’s obeisance and reclaim the Senate’s authority to influence the department’s direction.

“The country needs an attorney general who will check the worst impulses of this administration,” Ms. Murkowski said on Friday. “I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case.”

Shortly after, Mr. Cassidy took to the floor to offer Mr. Blanche his support.

The floor fight over Mr. Blanche was preceded by a clash in the Senate Judiciary Committee that followed a similar trajectory.

Two lame-duck senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, briefly withheld their support on the Senate Judiciary Committee over Mr. Blanche’s role in a deal to resolve Mr. Trump’s lawsuit against the I.R.S. The ensuing agreement created a $1.8 billion fund to compensate purported victims of Biden-era abuses at the department and granted Mr. Trump sweeping immunity from tax investigations.

Both made it clear, from the start, that they liked Mr. Blanche and did not consider his reluctance to challenge Mr. Trump to be disqualifying.

They simply wanted him to put in writing his verbal commitment to kill the fund and to include modest limits on the tax provision. Mr. Blanche was amenable, but the White House resisted, and Mr. Trump threatened to temporarily withdraw Mr. Blanche’s nomination until the two lawmakers were out of office.

The president eventually relented, clearing the way for a vote on the floor. But the episode underscored, in the view of critics, the lopsided power dynamic inherent in the partnership between Mr. Trump and Mr. Blanche.

Mr. Cornyn expressed broader concerns about Mr. Blanche’s independence during a confirmation hearing last month, echoing Ms. Murkowksi’s statements.

But he did not withhold his vote to make the larger point as she did and confined his final senatorial stand to a narrower patch of ground — obtaining written assurances over the agreement that emerged from the I.R.S. suit.

After the Senate committee advanced Mr. Blanche’s nomination, Mr. Cornyn conceded that Mr. Trump, resentful of being forced to make even a modest accommodation, might backtrack on the agreement after he retired.

“There’s nothing we could do to rein in the president when he said he likes the fund and wishes it still exists, but the fact of the matter is it’s dead, and that’s all we could do under the circumstances,” he told reporters.

item.title: The U.S. Is Burning Through Weapons in Iran. Russia and China Are Taking Note.
item.description:
President Trump’s war against Iran has depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles to troubling levels, siphoning supplies from Asia and Europe, according to senior officials.

The rapidly shrinking supply of air-defense missiles and other critical weaponry in Europe and Asia not only leaves the U.S. military less equipped, but could also leave Russia and China feeling emboldened should they contemplate a potential conflict with the United States, experts said.

Bombing Iran burned through thousands of multimillion-dollar missiles that contain precision parts from a global web of suppliers and can take years to produce. Defending against Iran’s retaliatory barrages has worn down U.S. stocks of air-defense missiles to an extent that has privately alarmed top officials in the Trump administration and has led to the United States’ delaying deliveries to European and Asian customers.

The Iran campaign has forced the Pentagon to rush ships, aircraft and air-defense units from across Europe and Asia to the Middle East, an effort with cascading consequences for equipment maintenance and troop morale, U.S. officials said. The result is a significant erosion of American firepower in those regions, a shift with long-term implications that are a growing concern in the military and intelligence communities, senior U.S. and Western officials said.

Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, said the United States has “more than enough firepower to carry out any operation the president orders at any time and place.” But experts say the munitions crisis — part of which Mr. Trump inherited from President Joseph R. Biden Jr. — is almost certain to outlast his presidency.

Tom Karako, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, said the depletion of munitions was a “generational annihilation of the means of conventional deterrence.” The impact on how decisions are made in Beijing and Moscow, he said, could resonate for years.

“It’s impossible for that not to have a significant effect on the decision calculus of Russia and China,” said Mr. Karako, who has been tracking U.S. weapons stockpiles. “They may do something quite deliberate and at the time of their choosing, because keep in mind — we’re going to take years to reconstitute.”

In meetings in the lead-up to the Iran war, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, informed the president of the risks of dipping deeper into drained stockpiles, according to two officials with knowledge of the exchanges. Mr. Trump still decided to go ahead, believing the war would be over quickly. A spokesman for General Caine declined to comment on his private conversations with the president.

After attacking Iran alongside Israel on Feb. 28, Mr. Trump repeatedly promised victory within weeks. More than five months later, he remains unable to bend Iran to his will, or even to find a way to end the war. The munitions shortage is said to have played a role in persuading Mr. Trump to put aside a major bombing campaign late last month. But it also shows how the president’s decision to attack Iran has left the United States and its allies more vulnerable to other threats.

The Trump administration has worked with military contractors to try to accelerate and expand production. But even accounting for those efforts, it could take more than two years for the United States to replenish the more than 1,500 Patriot air-defense interceptor missiles that have been used in the Iran war. The current U.S. inventory of those missiles is fewer than 1,700, according to two people briefed on the stockpile who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military details.

Mr. Trump has been enraged about news stories covering the munitions shortages. He has ordered a massive leak hunt across his government and is demanding criminal prosecutions. He has told advisers in private that any discussion of the munitions crisis signals weakness to the country’s enemies, and he continues in public to downplay the issue, deny it exists or blame his predecessor.

“Our defense companies are making more munitions than ever before, while rapidly expanding their plants and equipment at record levels,” Ms. Leavitt, the White House press secretary, said in a statement. “Anyone entrusted with access to classified military information who leaks it to the media is betraying that trust and breaking federal law, and should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesman, said reports of weapons shortages are false, adding that the United States has “everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing.”

The most immediate impact of the munitions shortage is being felt in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said this week that the number of air-defense missiles being provided to his country by Western allies had dropped threefold this year compared with 2025. On Wednesday, Ukraine failed to intercept any of the 28 missiles fired by Russia, which killed at least 17 people. More interceptors, Mr. Zelensky said, “could have saved the lives of those killed today.”

The fundamental problem, analysts say, is that Russia has ramped up its missile production to a greater extent than Ukraine’s Western supporters have been able to manufacture air defenses. The Iran war exacerbated the mismatch.

Representative Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat who sits on the House Armed Services and Intelligence Committees, said the “antiquated” U.S. defense procurement process “doesn’t allow us to actually keep pace with the rapidly evolving nature of warfare.”

“Frankly, our adversaries don’t have those hindrances,” Mr. Crow said.

The United States and its allies have begun to hoard air-defense missiles amid the global supply crunch. Mr. Trump, asked by a reporter in the Oval Office on Thursday about Mr. Zelensky’s plea for more missiles, shot back: “We want missiles too.”

Mr. Trump regularly insists that Mr. Biden’s support for Ukraine is to blame for any shortfalls in U.S. weapons stocks. He said on social media on Thursday that the United States had “massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types.”

It is true that the United States has a vast arsenal of less advanced munitions, including more than 100,000 guided bombs that are dropped from aircraft, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The problem with many of those weapons is that they have to be released close to their targets, putting more warplanes at risk of getting shot down.

High-end cruise missiles avoid that risk because they can be launched from hundreds of miles away. But the U.S. military largely exhausted its stocks of certain types of long-range missiles — such as the Army Tactical Missile Systems, or ATACMS, and Precision Strike Missiles — during the Iran war, officials said.

Long-range missiles would be critical in a war against China or Russia, countries with far more advanced air defenses than Iran. Both governments are tracking U.S. stockpiles closely, estimating them through public sources like the congressional budget process and defense contractor announcements, as well as via their spy satellites and other surveillance systems, according to a U.S. official familiar with defense intelligence.

“The situation is shaping up very favorably,” a popular Russian pro-war blogger, Aleksandr Kots, recently wrote. “The less precision-guided weaponry the U.S. has, the less will reach Ukraine.”

Even if Mr. Trump’s successor wants to ramp up aid to Ukraine, Mr. Kots added, “doing so will be impossible with empty arsenals.”

The long-term impact of the depletion may be greatest in Asia, where the United States has long been preparing for the possibility of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, the self-governing island that Beijing claims as its own. The U.S. military’s Indo-Pacific Command became a major source of munitions for the Iran war, with many of its Tomahawks and other long-range missiles in the region — critical to a fight with China — transferred from its stocks.

Hundreds of advanced air-defense interceptors have been sent to the Middle East from South Korea and elsewhere in Asia, while a carrier strike group and some of the Navy’s highest-end destroyers were deployed from the region to support the Iran campaign. U.S. troops in South Korea would be more vulnerable in a war with North Korea because the Pentagon has redirected tactical surveillance assets to the Middle East and withdrawn air defenses, a U.S. official said.

The depletion has wide-ranging effects. In Asia, some U.S. officials fear that South Korea and Japan will doubt the ability of the United States to protect them with nonnuclear defenses, and will be more inclined to seek their own nuclear weapons to establish more credible deterrence. In Europe, U.S. allies are already looking to increase weapons purchases from other countries, given the production backlog in the United States.

Russia and China have long understood that the U.S. stockpile is limited, officials say, and now understand that inventories will take time to be refilled to levels that would allow for the execution of certain war plans. In that sense, a more drawn-out Iran conflict benefits Moscow and Beijing, some analysts said.

“The longer this war runs and the more we continue to exchange fire with Iran, the worse the munitions problem becomes for the United States, and the larger and more visible this window of vulnerability becomes,” said Todd Harrison, a defense analyst at the American Enterprise Institute.

Dara Massicot, an expert on the Russian military at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that Moscow had already been reassessing its assumptions about U.S. military stockpiles before the start of the Iran war. The four years of conflict in Ukraine, she said, might have shown Russian military planners that the United States was slower at ramping up weapons production than they had believed.

“That’s the wrong kind of math to go into the Russian system, because then they start changing their perception of their own power vis-à-vis NATO,” said Ms. Massicot, who recently returned from a trip to Ukraine. “It causes them to come to conclusions that we may not want them to.”

Xinyun Wu contributed reporting from Taipei.

item.title: Flesh-Eating Bacteria Kills 5 in Louisiana
item.description:
Louisiana health officials said that five residents died this year after they were sickened with Vibrio vulnificus, a flesh-eating bacteria that thrives in warm seas and brackish water.

Vibrio bacteria occur naturally in coastal waters, and people can be infected with the pathogen when an open wound comes into contact with the water or when they consume undercooked shellfish, particularly oysters. Another four people in the state were hospitalized with the infection, health officials said this week.

All nine of the cases reported in Louisiana were associated with wounds exposed to seawater, officials said.

Vibrio are more common from May through October, when seawater tends to be warmer. In recent years, however, outbreaks have occurred in places once thought to be too cold to support the bacteria, such as Long Island Sound, in part due to climate change.

Researchers from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Environmental Protection Agency have estimated that U.S. cases of Vibrio infections could increase by 50 percent by 2090 compared with 1995 because of higher sea temperatures.

About a dozen different Vibrio species can cause a human illness called vibriosis, with Vibrio vulnificus being one of the most common, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The C.D.C. estimates that 80,000 cases of vibriosis happen every year in the United States.

About one in five people who contract Vibrio vulnificus die, sometimes within a day or two of becoming ill, the C.D.C. said. Symptoms of an infection include diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever. If the infection moves into the bloodstream, it can also cause low blood pressure and blistering skin lesions.

In Louisiana, all the patients had underlying health conditions, which can increase the risk of severe infections or complications.

Other states have also reported Vibrio vulnificus this year. In Florida, two people have died from the pathogen, one in Marion County in Central Florida and one in Palm Beach, according to the Florida Department of Health. In total, 14 people in the state have been sickened by it, the department reported. And in April, researchers in New York said they had detected Vibrio vulnificus in several bodies of water off the coast of Long Island.

Florida health officials warned that risk of exposure to the bacteria increases after severe weather events, such as storms and hurricanes that push brackish water inland. In 2024, the year of Hurricane Helene and Milton, the state reported 19 deaths from Vibrio vulnificus.

Health officials in Louisiana warned the public to stay out of brackish or saltwater if they had open wounds and to wash them thoroughly with soap after possible exposure. They also encouraged people to cook seafood thoroughly and to keep cooked seafood separate from raw seafood and its juices.

item.title: Internal Report on Avalanche That Killed 9 Skiers Assigns No Blame
item.description:
A report commissioned by the guide company that was leading a backcountry ski party near Lake Tahoe in February when an avalanche killed nine skiers attributed no direct blame to the company.

The report details the movements of the group of backcountry skiers led by Blackbird Mountain Guides after it left the Frog Lake Huts, near Donner Pass, during a major snowstorm on Feb. 17.

It leans on previously reported news media accounts, the GPS tracks of two party members and avalanche and weather data. It includes accounts of Blackbird guides, including the lone surviving guide as well as the owner, Zeb Blais, who was not on the trip but joined the search-and-rescue effort.

The report draws no conclusions and does not say if mistakes were made. And it does not ask or address a key question: Why did the 15-member group leave the huts in the snowstorm rather than staying sheltered?

The exact cause of the avalanche remains unclear.

“It is not known, nor will ever be known, whether the avalanche was naturally triggered, or triggered by the weight of the group,” the report said.

The aftermath of the avalanche has been clouded by possible legal ramifications for Blackbird and Blais. The sheriff’s department for Nevada County, where the avalanche occurred, said on Friday that the case remained open and was under review by the district attorney. Civil lawsuits from victims or families are possible, too, though none have been filed.

On Thursday, the sheriff’s department released heavily redacted coroner reports for the nine victims. All died of asphyxia “due to burial in snow during avalanche,” the coroner said.

The report contains two parts. The bulk is an “independent preliminary report” prepared by Don Sharaf, former owner of the American Avalanche Institute, a Colorado-based company that has taught safety courses for more than 50 years.

The other is a “supplemental document” prepared by Blackbird, highlighting some of the “key findings.” Among them, Blackbird said, was the route selection, which has been the subject of great speculation.

Blackbird, with dozens of guides, taught avalanche-safety courses and regularly took clients on overnight trips to Frog Lake. The chosen route on Feb. 17 was the one most frequently used by Blackbird. A meeting on the morning of the avalanche included discussion of giving a wide berth to the northern slopes of Perry’s Peak, where the avalanche occurred, the report said.

Using the GPS tracks of one of the deceased guides and one of the surviving clients, the report posits that the group tried to cross a small creek multiple times, away from a known avalanche zone and toward relatively safer terrain, “but were most likely turned back by open water and vertical creek sidewalls.”

Blackbird’s supplement highlights that possibility.

“Based on the group’s tracks from the preceding days, they would not have known about this impassable barrier before their exit on Tuesday morning,” the supplement said.

Two of the survivors, Jim Hamilton and Anton Auzans, said on Saturday that they did not recall any attempts or discussions about crossing the creek, though both men were at the tail end of the group. Neither was interviewed for the report, nor were other survivors besides the guide Ryan Tilley.

Other possible routes from the huts that morning were potentially more problematic, the company said. They were longer and also included avalanche exposure, while skirting private property, the report said.

Blackbird wrote in its part of the report that it had followed established risk-management practices “including terrain and route selection, continued assessment of weather and snowpack conditions, and careful management of exposure.”

It added: “Guiding under elevated avalanche hazard is a recognized and accepted professional practice when these methods are applied.”

Blackbird had two groups of clients scheduled to stay for two nights at the Frog Lake Huts, which are owned by the Truckee Donner Land Trust and have been open to the public since late 2021.

One group had eight women, mostly from the Bay Area, led by two guides. The other had three men, unknown to one another before the trip, led by another two guides.

On the clear morning of Sunday, Feb. 15, with a strong multiday snowstorm forecast to arrive that night, the groups left from Donner Pass near Interstate 80. They skied north for several miles to reach the heated huts, passing not far from where the avalanche happened two days later.

The groups skied independently that afternoon and in the fresh snow on Monday. On Tuesday morning, the day of departure, a planned ski run before returning home was called off because of heavy snow and wind. The groups were combined and they set off together.

Less than two hours after leaving the huts, the avalanche buried most of the skiers. Six of the women and three of the four guides were killed.

“There is nothing easy about any part of this,” the guide company said in a statement on Saturday. “Nine deeply loved people are gone, three of them our own guides. There is still much that remains unknown, but this is the most complete information available so far and we hope the release of this information can help the community begin to heal together.”

David Choo, father of Nicole Choo, one of the guides who died, said the report contained information that was already known. “Nothing in the report changes our view that this was a tragic accident,” he said.

His hope, he said, is that others will learn from it.

“Backcountry skiing will always be inherently risky,” he said. “It is only through more education of the entire industry and community, both individually and as collectives, that we can minimize the loss of lives through avalanches.”

item.title: Senate Bows to Reality, Leaving Trump’s Voting Bill Undone
item.description:
The Senate bowed to political reality at 4:36 a.m. on Saturday, adjourning and allowing bleary-eyed senators to leave Washington without any concrete steps toward passing the voting restriction bill that President Trump has demanded for months.

Republican lawmakers had insisted they would work tirelessly to enact election changes that Mr. Trump has suggested the party needs in place to win the midterm elections. Instead, they departed with little to show for their efforts, other than a performative pre-dawn procedural vote on a watered-down version of the bill that they knew they could not pass.

Even the staunchest advocates of the election measure eventually conceded what had been clear all along: There was simply not enough Republican support to push through the strict voter identification legislation. With the party’s majority at risk, senators were eager to abandon the futile effort so they could get home to their states to campaign for re-election.

“We are not in a position right now where we have the wherewithal to pass it right now,” Senator Mike Lee, Republican of Utah and one of the most forceful proponents of the legislation, said on Friday night.

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, had been making that case for months, alluding in increasingly blunt terms to “math” and “reality” that he suggested the president simply did not appreciate as Mr. Trump angrily demanded the Senate find a way to pass the elections bill.

The president’s proposed measure would require Americans to show proof of citizenship to register to vote, impose a nationwide voter identification requirement and severely limit voting by mail. That legislation, which the president has called the SAVE America Act, has neither the majority it would need to pass nor the 60 votes needed to overcome a Democratic filibuster.

Still, Mr. Trump commanded the Senate to cancel its planned five-week recess if it did not pass the measure. Mr. Lee had been one of his loudest allies, threatening to block the Senate from adjourning or force his colleagues to go on the record with a politically unappealing vote in favor of leaving Washington for the summer rather than staying at work at the Capitol.

But in the end, Mr. Lee did neither. Though he forced the Senate to vote to adjourn, he accepted a voice vote that did not require senators to formally register a position.

In a late push to show progress on the elections measure, Republican leaders had rushed to draft a $150 billion budget blueprint to fund the war with Iran and the implementation of new election restrictions, and discussed bringing it to a vote. That plan would pave the way for filibuster-proof legislation known as a reconciliation bill to bypass Democratic opposition.

But it was clear that the measure would have failed overnight, lacking enough support among Republicans to move ahead.

Senator Ron Johnson, Republican of Wisconsin and the chairman of the Budget Committee, said that lawmakers would postpone the effort until they return in September. He and other senators called Mr. Trump to tell him of the plan, which they said he supported.

“We’re in total agreement,” Mr. Johnson said on Friday night. “We were just kind of like, ‘Here’s the reality.’ He would like a better reconciliation bill that will take more time, so he was completely supportive of it.”

But the budget reconciliation process is cumbersome, and Republicans are running out of time to pass their measure before Election Day. The Senate has just three scheduled weeks in Washington before the midterm elections, in which control of Congress is at stake.

Senators who are up for re-election were particularly eager to return home so they can focus on making their cases to voters. Senator Lisa Murkowski pointed to several competitive races, including that of Senator Dan Sullivan, her fellow Alaska Republican, as she made the case for adjourning.

“The most important thing for Senator Sullivan as well as my friend Susan Collins and Jon Husted and Pete Ricketts is for them to be able to go home and be in their states and go to work again,” Ms. Murkowski said, referring to Republican senators in Maine, Ohio and Nebraska who must face voters in November.

Before they left, Republicans held a test vote meant to put Democrats on the defensive on the voter ID piece of the elections bill, seizing upon an idea that polls have shown is broadly popular. They tried to advance a bill sponsored by Mr. Husted, who is facing a difficult re-election race, that would have required voters nationwide to show certain forms of photo identification in federal elections.

Ultimately, the effort failed on a party-line vote, with all Democrats voting against it.

Though some Democrats have said they support federal voter ID requirements, they have argued that Mr. Husted’s measure would too strictly limit what forms of identification were acceptable, potentially blocking eligible voters who lacked the proper documentation from being able to cast ballots.

Catie Edmondson and Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

item.title: Bill Goichberg, Who Reshaped Competitive Chess in the U.S., Dies at 83
item.description:
Bill Goichberg, the foremost chess impresario in the United States, whose ideas about organizing tournaments reshaped and expanded competitive chess over his six-decade career, died on Sunday. He was 83.

His death was announced by the U.S. Chess Federation, the game’s governing body. No further details were provided.

Tall and imposing, with a distinctive, nasally voice that rose when he got into a dispute with a player in one of the tournaments he ran — when, for example, a player who had been designated to play black insisted that he should play white, which has the advantage of moving first — Mr. Goichberg thought outside the box about who might be interested in playing competitive chess. He also bet bigger on chess as a business than anyone had before.

The results were clear: According to the Continental Chess Association, which Mr. Goichberg founded in the 1960s, by 2018, the most recent date for which statistics were available, the association had held more than 2,300 tournaments and awarded over $24 million in prize money.

In 1966, Mr. Goichberg organized the first scholastic tournament rated by the U.S. Chess Federation. Before that, scholastic tournaments had been unrated — meaning that they were not counted for official rankings — because organizers believed that students would not be willing to be pay membership dues to the federation.

That turned out not to be the case; far from it. In April 1966, at the Greater New York scholastics championships, there were 253 competitors, of which 134 were new federation members. The scholastic championships that December had 614 players — more than double the previous record for a scholastic tournament — and about 400 of those competitors were new members.

The same year, Mr. Goichberg organized the first tournament for elementary-school children. At the time, the consensus was that children that young — with the exception of the occasional prodigy — were not interested in playing chess. Over the next several decades, elementary tournaments would become the most popular format for scholastic chess.

In 1969, Mr. Goichberg organized the first national high-school championship. Held in New York City, it attracted 370 players from 21 states. Four years later, he started the national junior-high championship — and, in 1976, the national elementary-school championship.

Those three tournaments, now run by the U.S. Chess Federation, have been held every year since they debuted; together, they usually have more than 5,000 competitors.

In 1991, Mr. Goichberg started a tournament to crown champions from kindergarten through 12th grade. That tournament, which routinely attracts between 1,500 and 2,000 competitors, is now also run by the federation.

Opening the door to scholastic chess transformed the federation. As of late last month, 54,116 members, or nearly half of the total of 113,271 members, were younger than 18.

In 1973, Mr. Goichberg organized the World Open, a tournament open to anyone, with a total prize fund of $15,000 (over $110,000 today), more than 50 percent higher than that of any previous tournament.

The first event had 732 competitors. In subsequent years, the tournament grew, routinely attracting more than 1,000 players, with a peak of 1,506 in 1986, a record for an open tournament that still stands.

Though other tournaments emerged with prize funds that eventually surpassed that of the World Open, it remains the oldest and largest continually organized open tournament in the world. Spurred by its success, Mr. Goichberg started other major annual tournaments, including the Chicago Open and the North American Open.

For decades, talented American players who wanted to earn international titles — particularly grandmaster, the most coveted — had to play in Europe because there were not enough tournaments in the United States that satisfied the requirements, known as norms.

In 1976, Mr. Goichberg began organizing tournaments that allowed American players to gain international ratings and norms. Over the years, he also expanded some of his large open tournaments to nine rounds, the minimum necessary for players to earn norms. Generations of talented Americans, including Joel Benjamin, a three-time U.S. champion, earned their first international rankings and norms in Goichberg-run tournaments.

William Goichberg was born on Nov. 11, 1942, in Manhattan, the eldest of two children of Sol and Fannie (Lieberman) Goichberg, immigrants who both played the mandolin. Sol, a virtuoso mandolin player, met Fannie when she was one of his students. A talented mandolinist in her own right, she eventually played in the New York Mandolin Orchestra.

When Bill was young, the Goichbergs moved to Mount Vernon, N.Y., where he grew up. He learned to play chess from his father when he was about 2, according to Jon Jacobs, a chess master and coach who is working on a book about Mr. Goichberg.

When he was 12, his father bought him a subscription to Chess Review, one of the two main chess periodicals in the United States. He also read all the chess books in the local library.

He played his first tournament in 1961 and was a master by 1964, the same year that he achieved the distinction of playing the third-most tournament games of anyone in the country. He also began working as a statistician for the U.S. Chess Federation. In 1966, he became co-editor of Chess Life, Chess Review’s principal competitor.

Mr. Goichberg began organizing tournaments as a young man, out of frustration. In 1962, he played in the New York City Junior Championship, but failed to capture the title. He wanted to play the next year, his final year of eligibility (the tournament was for players under 21), but the competition was not held.

He decided that he would remedy the situation by organizing the 1964 tournament himself. It attracted 34 players, 10 more than in 1962. Then he organized the 1965 tournament, which brought in 92 players.

Though he continued to play — even becoming a FIDE master, the third-highest title awarded by the International Chess Federation — Mr. Goichberg became increasingly focused on organizing. He played his last full tournament in 1983.

In early 1964, he founded the New York City Chess Association as a vehicle for organizing tournaments. Four years later, as his ambitions expanded, he changed the name to the Continental Chess Association.

In 2004, he became the U.S. Chess Federation’s executive director; a year later, he was named its president and served in that position until 2008.

He married Brenda L. Tersine in 1993. She was an expert in mortuary science, but joined him in running the Continental Chess Association. She died in 2022. He is survived by his sister, Rena Goichberg.

“He’s almost certainly the most important U.S. chess organizer of at least the last 50 years,” Dennis Monokroussos, a master who runs the blog The Chess Mind, wrote in a tribute after Mr. Goichberg’s death. “And you’ll probably need binoculars to spot whoever the number two organizer might happen to be.”

Ash Wu contributed reporting.

item.title: Firefighting Helicopter Crashes Near Utah Wildfire, Killing Two Onboard
item.description:
A helicopter battling one of the nation’s largest active wildfires crashed while navigating treacherous terrain in central Utah on Friday, killing the two firefighters who were on board, according to federal officials.

The aircraft, one of several fighting the fast-spreading Widemouth 2 blaze burning through Fishlake National Forest and the surrounding communities, went down near the city of Richfield around 10 a.m. The wreck sparked another fire, officials said, and flames quickly overran the area, initially preventing emergency personnel from reaching the site.

“No escape routes that any firefighters could get into or out of if we had put them in there,” said Nathan Curtis, the sheriff of Sevier County, where the crash occurred.

Overnight, the authorities remained uncertain about the fate of the pilot and crew member aboard the helicopter, which had been working on contract with the U.S. Forest Service, but by Saturday morning their worst fears had been confirmed.

The National Interagency Fire Center, a coalition of federal and state agencies, reported their deaths in its daily bulletin.

Officials have not identified the firefighters, and they were still working to determine the cause of the crash. Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board traveled to the area but were waiting for fire conditions to improve before they could reach the crash site, said a spokeswoman for the agency, Sarah Taylor Sulick.

In an unsigned statement, the Forest Service said only that it was “an emerging situation” and that “safety actions are prioritized first.”

But even as many central questions remained unanswered, Friday’s fatalities deepened an already solemn mood that has taken hold at base camps and incident command centers across the West this year, as a raging wildfire season has claimed the lives of several other first responders. In June, three wildland firefighters died while battling a blaze along the Utah-Colorado border, and on Thursday a bulldozer operator was killed in a southern Oregon fire.

“Wildland firefighting is among the most dangerous jobs in the world,” Gov. Spencer Cox of Utah said in a statement on Friday, responding to the crash in his state. “Today is a painful reminder of the extraordinary risks these brave men and women accept to protect us.”

Authorities believe the Widemouth 2 fire began with a lightning strike on July 27 and quickly scorched more than 100,000 acres, feasting on tinder-dry forests and propelled by unpredictable winds. It is the latest large blaze in what researchers say is one of the state’s worst fire seasons on record, with Utah — and the rest of the West — struggling through a brutal drought and sweltering summer.

“This is our third fire to be right at 100,000 acres this year, which is not a record that we’re proud of,” Mr. Cox told reporters during a tour of the fire line on Thursday. He said the fierce fire season had exhausted emergency workers and spread resources thin.

When the firefighting helicopter, a Sikorsky S64, took off on Friday morning, conditions were safe enough to fly, Tyler Hecht, a deputy commander with the Great Basin Incident Management Team, said at a news briefing later that day. The terrain was steep and tricky, Mr. Hecht said, but it was not unusual for this type of wildfire.

As Widemouth 2 continued to rage, with just about a quarter of the blaze contained, officials were left hoping for rain — just not too much, as communities near fire burn scars are now fearing flash floods and mudslides.

“Really,” Mr. Cox said, “we need some help from Mother Nature.”

Madaleine Rubin contributed reporting.

item.title: Hunter Biden Says His Father’s Cancer Is Worsening
item.description:
Former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body, leaving him in pain, his son Hunter Biden said in an interview broadcast on Friday.

“It’s metastasized into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden told a BBC journalist. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating, in many respects.”

The former president, 83, was diagnosed in May 2025 with an aggressive form of prostate cancer, his office revealed at the time. Last year, he had surgery to remove skin cancer lesions and completed a round of radiation therapy. His daughter, Ashley Biden, posted a video of Mr. Biden ringing a bell, a tradition that patients perform to mark a major treatment milestone.

The diagnosis did not prevent Mr. Biden from making some public appearances. He recently delivered the keynote address at a fund-raising event for the Maryland Democratic Party, on what happened to be the two-year anniversary of a disastrous presidential debate performance that effectively ended his re-election campaign.

“He’s still out there,” Hunter Biden said in the interview broadcast on Friday. “As long as he’s alive, I promise you, he is going to continue to fight.”

Prostate cancer is typically a slow-growing disease that affects older men, and can be present for years without symptoms or a diagnosis. Advanced cases often spread to the bones, like the former president’s has, Jill Biden, his wife and the former first lady, said in a podcast interview this week with Kelly Ripa, the talk-show host. Once the cancer gets in the bones, medical experts say, it cannot be cured.

Dr. Biden said that her husband’s treatment was ongoing.

“He will forever live with cancer,” Dr. Biden said. “It’s constant. It’s daily. And I think it’s challenging.”

Mr. Biden, who has long supported cancer research, has already dealt with family tragedy related to the disease. His son Beau died in 2015 of glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer.

Mr. Biden has had many health problems, including a brain aneurysm in 1988 that threatened to end his political career.

The former president plans to release a memoir titled “Promise Me, America” shortly after the November midterm elections.

item.title: Max Miller, Republican Accused of Abuse, Won’t Drop Out, Spokeswoman Says
item.description:
Representative Max Miller, the Republican from Ohio accused of physically abusing his ex-wife and young daughter, has defied calls from his own party to drop out and plans to stay in the race to keep his seat in Congress, according to his spokeswoman.

Mr. Miller would have had to withdraw by Saturday evening, at the latest, to allow local party chairs enough time to name a replacement on the ballot by Monday at 4 p.m., according to Ohio state law.

His decision, confirmed by Abigail Angelos, a campaign spokeswoman, sets up a competitive general-election campaign. Mr. Miller’s district was considered solidly Republican before his divorce from the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio and the public allegations of physical abuse that followed.

Mr. Miller has denied the accusations, which include holding a gun to his ex-wife’s head, throwing scalding water at her and fracturing the collarbone of their daughter.

Over the past week, pressure mounted from within his party for him to step aside. President Trump called Mr. Miller, a former aide to the president, to encourage him to look carefully at his odds. Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican also up for re-election, described him as unfit for office and urged him to resign from Congress. White House staff members and Republican officials in Ohio have privately conveyed concerns that his personal problems could cost the party a seat as it tries to keep control of the House.

But Mr. Miller has been resolute all week that he planned to do what Mr. Trump had done when faced with his own personal scandals: stay in and fight. He has defended himself in a media tour that left some in his own party worried about his mental state and alarmed at the prospect of his continued candidacy.

In November, he will face Brian Poindexter, a union-card-carrying ironworker who Democrats believe can defeat Mr. Miller with an appeal to the working-class voters in Ohio’s Seventh District.

The Ohio Republican Party and local party chairs stayed publicly quiet this week, for the most part, declining to answer questions about whether they supported Mr. Miller’s candidacy.

If Mr. Miller had withdrawn, they would have had to call a meeting by the end of Saturday to replace him, under state law.

Matt Miller, the chairman of the Ashland County Republican Party and the mayor of Ashland, who is not related to the congressman, said on Saturday that no such meeting had been scheduled.

item.title: Beth, the Beloved Vacuum of a 92-Year-Old Iowa Senator, Has Died
item.description:
Beth, a trusty tan Hoover vacuum cleaner with a burgundy cloth dust bag that for years tended to the floors of the Iowa farmhouse of Senator Chuck Grassley, earning admirers in both parties, has died. She was believed to be 49.

The cause was apparently an electrical problem, said Mr. Grassley, a Republican who often admiringly posted images of his cleaning companion on social media around Christmas, Thanksgiving, Easter and family reunions.

“U willl see Beth no more,” Mr. Grassley, 92 and the oldest senator, wrote on social media on Saturday, attaching an image that showed Beth’s electrical cord connector scarred by sparks. “See black that’s from electrical sparks. It’s not safe to use anymore. GOOD BYE BETH.”

It’s a sad day at Grassley household…. For my 34 years and 15 yrs before that at my mother in law’s home Beth has worked dependably….

He declared it a “sad day at Grassley household” and recalled that Beth had worked “dependably” for 34 years at his home, and for 15 years before that at his mother-in-law’s house. He wrote of Beth, “U hv been a real workhorse,” adding, “I will miss u.”

Year after year, around the holidays and during other occasions when cleaning was in order, Mr. Grassley would fire up Beth. The vacuum, he said, allowed him to make a contribution to the festivities as others in the family prepared food.

At roughly 49, Beth had been at work since before Mr. Grassley, a corn and soybean farmer, reached the Senate in 1981. The vacuum was also older than several U.S. senators.

But Beth drew public notice only in recent years, when Mr. Grassley, who has an irreverent style on social media, began to post about his vacuum. (In 2020, Mr. Grassley announced the death of a pigeon by writing on social media, “If u lost ur pet pidgin /it’s dead in front yard my Iowa farm JUST DISCOVERED.”)

Two days before Thanksgiving in 2018, Mr. Grassley wrote on social media: “Mrs G and daughter Wendy hv started big job of preparing meal for30 at farm Thxgiving. So my housework contribution begins. This is my machine (Beth).”

He made a habit of such posts.

“Faithful Beth has about 3 hours of cleaning to get ready for 25/30 grassley family,” he wrote on Christmas in 2022.

For Thanksgiving in 2023, he shared a video of Beth roaring across a rug as he pushed the vacuum and shuffled behind it.

The same year, Mr. Grassley posted an image of him and Senator Shelley Moore Capito, Republican of West Virginia, holding a cutout image of Beth. “Turns out Senator Capito is a big fan of Beth,” he wrote.

Beth had, by any measure, an extraordinarily long life for an upright vacuum cleaner. A typical vacuum might last for eight years, according to Consumer Reports, though life spans vary by brand.

Hoover says that its upright vacuums last eight years on average, and that its cordless vacuums are good for about five years on average.

Techtronic Industries, which owns Hoover, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Beth’s demise.

But within hours of Mr. Grassley’s announcement, others in politics had begun to take note, and to offer condolences.

“Sorry for your loss, Senator,” Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative in Iowa running for the state’s other Senate seat, wrote Saturday evening on social media. “Sounds like Beth had a heck of a run.”
